summary: This RFC specifies the protocols and procedures a service provider uses so IP multicast traffic inside a BGP/MPLS IP VPN can travel from one VPN site to another. It is the core description of multicast VPNs on that kind of network.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 6513 describes how a service provider carries a customer's multicast traffic between sites in a BGP/MPLS VPN. It gives providers choices that trade off how precisely traffic is delivered against how much state core routers must keep.

questions: how does multicast work over mpls vpn
subtitle: How service providers carry customer multicast traffic between sites in BGP/MPLS VPNs.

tldr.problem: BGP/MPLS IP VPNs carry unicast between customer sites, but need additional procedures to carry multicast. Per-flow trees can also require too much state in provider core routers.
tldr.mechanism: Provider-edge routers discover VPN membership and exchange multicast routing information. P-multicast tunnels carry packets using inclusive or selective services, or ingress replication.
tldr.outcome: Providers can choose how to balance routing precision and core state, including per-flow choices. RFC 6513 has been updated by RFC 7582, RFC 7900 and RFC 7988.

today: RFC 6513 is a Proposed Standard and has been updated by RFC 7582, RFC 7900 and RFC 7988. RFC 6514 contains the detailed BGP encodings and procedures.

sections.title: Multicast Between VPN Sites
sections.content:
RFC 4364 defines BGP/MPLS IP VPN service for carrying customer unicast traffic between sites. RFC 6513 extends that service to carry IP multicast traffic, creating a Multicast VPN (MVPN).

The customer-edge router at each site forms a multicast routing relationship with its provider-edge router. Customer-edge routers at separate sites do not become routing neighbors of each other. This specification describes a framework and procedures; the companion RFC 6514 gives the detailed BGP encodings and procedures.
sections.plainLanguage: A provider-edge router receives multicast traffic from a customer site and carries it to other sites in the same VPN. The customer routers do not need direct routing relationships with each other.

sections.title: Balancing Delivery Precision and Core State
sections.content:
To route each multicast flow optimally, provider core routers would need state for each source-and-group flow. The provider cannot control how many groups, sources, or receivers its customers have, so this state could grow without bound.

RFC 6513 allows a provider to aggregate traffic on inclusive trees, which may deliver packets to provider-edge routers that do not need them. Selective trees reach fewer routers but require more core state. With ingress replication, the sending provider-edge router sends a unicast copy to each receiving router; core routers keep no multicast routing state, but the sender performs all copying.
sections.plainLanguage: A shared tree uses less core state but may carry traffic to sites that do not need it. A selective tree is more targeted, while ingress replication moves the copying work to the sending router.

sections.title: PMSIs and the Tunnels That Carry Them
sections.content:
A P-Multicast Service Interface (PMSI) is a service that delivers a packet from one provider-edge router to some or all other provider-edge routers in an MVPN. A receiving router can determine which VPN the packet belongs to. A P-tunnel is the transport mechanism that implements the PMSI.

An MVPN can have a multidirectional inclusive PMSI, where any router can send to every other router; a unidirectional inclusive PMSI, rooted at one router; or a selective PMSI, which reaches a subset. A P-tunnel may carry more than one PMSI if the packets include information that lets receiving routers distinguish them.
sections.plainLanguage: A PMSI describes which provider-edge routers can exchange traffic for an MVPN. A P-tunnel is the chosen transport that carries that traffic.

sections.title: Discovering VPN Members and Multicast Routes
sections.content:
BGP auto-discovery lets provider-edge routers learn which other routers belong to an MVPN. They advertise MCAST-VPN routes with route targets; a router that imports a matching route target can identify the advertising router as a member. The BGP encodings are specified in RFC 6514.

After discovering members, routers must exchange customer multicast routing information. RFC 6513 describes full PIM peering across a multidirectional inclusive PMSI and the use of BGP routes for source-tree and shared-tree joins. With full PIM peering, customer PIM control packets travel inside the provider tunnel and are not processed by provider core routers.
sections.plainLanguage: BGP advertisements tell provider-edge routers which VPNs other routers serve. The routers then exchange customer multicast routing information using PIM or BGP procedures.

sections.title: Aggregating VPN Traffic and Selecting Tunnels
sections.content:
One provider multicast tree can carry traffic for several MVPNs. Because the tree alone does not identify the VPN, the sending router adds an upstream-assigned MPLS label. The receiving router uses that label to select the correct VPN.

A provider-edge router may bind a particular customer multicast flow to a selective PMSI, for example to send it only to interested routers. The transmitting router chooses the tunnel. When changing tunnels, it waits for a switch-over delay and then sends on the new tunnel only, avoiding steady-state duplicate transmission.
sections.plainLanguage: A label identifies the VPN when multiple VPNs share one tunnel. A sender can move a flow to a more selective tunnel, but must stop sending it on the old tunnel after the switch.

sections.title: Crossing Provider Networks and Avoiding Duplicates
sections.content:
An MVPN can cross autonomous-system boundaries using segmented tunnels, whose separate segments are joined at border routers, or a non-segmented tunnel that spans the boundary. A non-segmented tunnel requires each autonomous system along its path to support the same tunnel technology.

Multihomed sources and changes from shared to source-specific trees can cause duplicate packets. Every MVPN must use at least one defined prevention method: discard packets arriving from a non-selected upstream router, select a single forwarder, or use native PIM methods. The RFC describes Source Active auto-discovery routes for a case where BGP carries multicast routing information.
sections.plainLanguage: Tunnels can cross provider boundaries as linked segments or as one continuous tunnel. Each MVPN must use a method that prevents duplicate packets from reaching customers.

sections.title: Control-Plane and Resource Protection
sections.content:
Provider routers must not accept PIM, mLDP, or RSVP-TE tunnel-building control messages from customer-edge routers. A provider-edge router must not accept MCAST-VPN BGP routes from a customer-edge router. An S-PMSI Join message received outside a PMSI must be discarded.

By default, an autonomous-system border router must not allow a P-tunnel to extend beyond the AS boundary; an operator can configure permitted interfaces. Implementations should also let providers limit customer multicast state and tunnel counts to reduce the risk of control-plane or data-plane overload.
sections.plainLanguage: Only provider routers may send messages that build provider tunnels. Providers also need limits on multicast state so unexpected customer activity does not overload routers.
